## Purpose and completion criteria

Assess whether the current simulation successfully handles union formation among men and women, across different model specifications.


| Measure | Comparison | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Mean age difference between partners | Compare to matching model specification | May not match exactly due to differences in male supply and eligibility requirements, but should shift in expected direction when model parameters change |
| Percent never married by age 50 | Comparison between gender and across specifications | Reasonable values and similar results for men and women | 
| percent ever married at age intervals | | | 
| SMAFM | | | 
| Preservation of TFR in on demand model | Comparison of observed TFR to input rate TFR | Close similarity between observed TFR and input rate TFR | 
| Matching Model Parameters     | Parameters to Estimates from Conditional Logit Model | Close similarity between parameters and estimates |
| Accounting and implementation | Existing tests | Successful unit tests |

## Overview of Design

Modeling union formation is complicated by the relationship between fertility and union formation. If women are only allowed to have children after being partnered, then the observed fertilty rates will fall below those of the input rates because women will spend some time not exposed to the risk of birth. This difference can be very substantial in modern populations where marriage happens late. This can be addressed by separating fertility rates into partnered fertility rates and unpartnered fertility rates, but this has requires more detailed input data (or stronger assumptions). 

### Searching Model

We handle this by providing two alternate models of when women search for a partner. In the first **on demand** case, partnerships are formed when a birth event would happend to an unpartnered women. Essentially, every union becomes a shotgun wedding. This approach will not produce realistic age specific marriage rates. However, it will ensure that input fertility rates are accurately reproduced in the simulation because it is the birth event that is "in the driver's seat." For researchers who are not concerned with modeling marriage specifically, this provides a very simple and straightforward option.

In the second **rate** case, we specify age specific partnership rates for women that compete with births and death as the next event. If a partnership search is assigned as the next event, then the woman will look for a partner using the same approach as in the **on demand** case. For the **rate** case, we also allow the user to specify in the fertility rates, an *unpartnered* and *partnered* schedule of fertility rates to better control overall fertility. This is not required, but if users do not specify these rates separately, then fertility rates and decisions will be completely independent of partnership status.

In both cases, it is the woman who initiates the search and then finds matches among men. We use this approach because it is substantially less complicated than a two-sided searching function with fewer data requirements.

### Matching Model

Once a decision is made to search for a partner, regardless of whether the **on demand** or **rate** model is used, a matching model based on a conditional logit model will be used. For a woman who is searching a sample of N unpartnered living men is drawn (N = 1000 by default but this can be modified). These men are then checked for eligibility. To be eligible they must:

- Be a certain minimum age (15 by default but adjustable by the user)
- They must not be kin within K generations of the woman. This defaults to two generations which rules out fathers, brothers, uncles, and first cousins. It can be set by the user.

All eligible men are then assigned a logit score based on model parameters that can be set by the user. Currently, only one variable - the age difference between partners - is available but additional variables will be added as the program develops. This age difference can be fit as a polynomial. The default setting uses a linear and quadratic term and allows the user to set the coefficients of each. So for example setting the linear term to 0.07 and the quadratic term to -0.014, would lead to a model where the likelihood of a union is maximized when the husband is 2.57 years older than the wife. 

These logit scores are then used to construct a probability for each eligible potential partner by:

EQUATION HERE 

The actual partner is then sampled from eligible partners with the probability provided above.

For the rate model, when unmarried fertility takes place, we also use this matching model to select a father for the birth, although this does not lead to a union. By default, the same matching model is used but users can also specify an alternate model.

## Inputs


For all validation checks, I will use rates from the USA circa 2000-2001. 

- Mortality rates come directly from the Human Mortality Database in one year intervals up to the open-ended interval at 110.
- All fertility rates, including unpartnered and partnered fertility rates, come from the NCHS report *Revised Birth and Fertility Rates for the 1990s and New Rates for Hispanic Populations, 2000 and 2001: United States*, NVSR 51(12), August 4, 2003, revised June 2004. These fertility rates are limited to the population aged 15-44, in five year age groups.
- Marriage rates come from the Census report, *Number, Timing, and Duration of Marriages and
Divorces: 2001* and are based on SIPP panel data. Marriage rates are recorded in five year age groups starting at age 15, with an open-ended group at age 70. Marriage rates are provided for both men and women. Only women's rates are used in the simulation, but I do also use the men's rates to compare to model output.

```{r}
#| label: get-input-data

# use HMD for mortality rates
mortality_rates <- get_mortality_hmd("USA", year = 2000)

# get total, partnered, and unpartnered fertility rates from 
# HCHS report data held in validation/data
fertility_rates_overall <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2000_fertility_overall.csv")
)
fertility_rates_by_status <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2000_fertility_by_union_status.csv")
)
mar_rates_female <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2001_marriage_rates_female.csv")
)
mar_rates_male <- read_csv(
  here("validation", "data", "usa_2001_marriage_rates_male.csv")
)

mar_rates_both <- bind_rows(
  mar_rates_female |> mutate(sex = "f"),
  mar_rates_male |> mutate(sex = "m")
)

time_breaks <- seq(2000, 2100, 5)
age_breaks <- seq(15, 70, 5)

fertility_rates_total |> calculate_tfr()
fertility_rates_by_status |> calculate_tfr()
```

Simulations are run for a hundred years starting from a base population that is uniformly distributed between zero and a hundred years. The starting population begins unmarried. A burn-in period is required before stable population dynamics will be achieved, but age-specific rates should be accurate from the beginning.

I also set up a matching model where the relativelikelihood of a union is given by:

$$0.072(\texttt{age_difference} - 0.014(\texttt{age_difference^2})$$

Where `age_difference` is the difference between potential husband's and wife's ages. The coefficients are derived from Gullickson (CITE) and come from US data (FROM WHEN?). Under this model the likelihood of a union will be maximized when the husband is 2.57 years older than the wife. Later, I will vary these parameters to confirm that they change the observed age differences between partners.

```{r}
#| label: set-settings

# beginning year of sim
start_time <- 2000
# years to run simulation
years <- 100
# ending time of the simulation
end_time <- start_time + years
# initial population construction parameters
population_size <- 100000
max_age <- 100
# minimum birth interval in years (0.75 = 9 months)
birth_interval <- 0.75
# seeds for random processes
population_seed <- 42
replication_seeds <- seq_len(100)
```

```{r}
#| label: initialize-model

set.seed(population_seed)
population <- create_baseline_population(
  population_size, max_age = max_age, end_time = start_time
)

model_base <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(population) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates)

model_matching <- create_matching_model(
  ~ age_difference + I(age_difference^2),
  c(age_difference = 0.072, "I(age_difference^2)" = -0.014)
)
```

## Evaluate On-Demand Model

To test the on-demand model, I run 100 separate simulations with the "on_demand" setting. I can then estimate average age-specific fertility rates, total fertility rates, marriage rates, and other characteristics across simulations.

```{r}
#| label: run-sim-ondemand

model_ondemand <- model_base |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates_overall) |>
  set_union_formation(
    "on_demand", 
    model_matching,
    diagnostics = TRUE
  )

results_ondemand <- map(replication_seeds, function(seed) {
  simulate(model_ondemand, years = years, seed = seed)
})
names(results_ondemand) <- as.character(replication_seeds)

counts_ondemand <- map(
  results_ondemand,
  calculate_lexis_counts,
  time_breaks,
  age_breaks,
  include_unions = TRUE
)

asfr <- counts_ondemand |> 
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  filter(sex == "f", age_start >= 15 & age_start < 45) |>
  group_by(union_status, age_start) |>
  summarize(
    rate = mean(rate_fertility),
    sd = sd(rate_fertility),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mar_rates <- counts_ondemand |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  filter(union_status == "unpartnered") |>
  group_by(age_start, sex) |>
  summarize(
    rate = mean(rate_marriage),
    sd = sd(rate_marriage),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tfr <- map(counts_ondemand, calculate_tfr) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2) |>
  group_by(time_mid, union_status) |>
  summarize(
    sd = sd(tfr),
    tfr = mean(tfr),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Fertility rates

The intent of the on-demand model is to preserve the age-specific fertility rates input by the user. Therefore, the first check is how closely the average observed age-specific fertility rates match those inputs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fertility-on-demand
#| fig-cap: Estimated mean age specific fertility rates across 100 simulations and 20 time periods compared to age specific fertility rates from input data. Red dotted line shows the input rates.

asfr |>
  filter(union_status == "overall") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start + 2.5, y = rate))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line(linetype = 1)+
  geom_line(data = fertility_rates_overall, linetype = 2, color = "red")+
  labs(x = "age", y = "fertility rate")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-fertility-on-demand shows the average age-specific fertility rates across all one hundred simulations in comparison to the expected input rates (shown by the dotted red line). The match is extremely good. As desired, the input fertility rates are being preserved in the simulations. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fertility-coverage
#| tbl-cap: Coverage of 95% confidence intervals for age-specific fertility rates by period.

counts_ondemand |> 
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  filter(sex == "f", age_start >= 15 & age_start < 45, union_status == "overall") |>
  select(time_start, time_end, age_start, age_end, rate_fertility) |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2) |>
  group_by(time_mid, age_start) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(rate_fertility),
    sd = sd(rate_fertility),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  inner_join(fertility_rates_overall, by = "age_start") |>
  mutate(
    upper = mean + 1.96 * se, lower = mean - 1.96 * se,
    include = rate <= upper & rate >= lower
  ) |>
  group_by(time_mid) |> 
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    coverage = mean(include),
    max_abs_deviation = max(abs(mean - rate)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    time_mid ~ "time period mid point",
    n ~ "age groups",
    coverage ~ "95% CI coverage",
    max_abs_deviation = "maximum absolute deviation"
  )
```

@tbl-fertility-coverage shows the share of age groups covered by the 95% confidence interval within each time period. With a small number of age groups, the coverage can be noisy, but the results here indicate a high level of coverage and very small maximum absolute deviation.  

Although the overall input fertility rates are preserved in the simulation output, I don't expect that the fertility rates disaggregated union status will match those empirically observed for the input case because the on demand model enforces a union on any birth to an unpartnered woman. @fig-union-status-fertility-on-demand shows the mean partnered and unpartnered age specific ferility rates observed in the simulation in comparison to those same rates from the input data. As expected, the results here are discrepant. Unpartnered fertility rates are forced to zero by the simulation and, to compensate, partnered fertility rates are higher than those actually observed. This finding does not invalidate the on demand model as it was expected, but users should be aware that this model cannot be used to generate reasonable partnered and unpartnered fertility rates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-union-status-fertility-on-demand
#| fig-cap: Estimated mean unpartnered and partnered age specific fertility rates across 100 simulations and 20 time periods compared to age specific fertility rates from input data. Points and dotted lines show empirically estimated rates and solid lines show input rates.

asfr |>
  filter(union_status != "overall") |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = age_start + 2.5, y = rate, 
    color = union_status, group = union_status
  ))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line(linetype = 2)+
  geom_line(data = fertility_rates_by_status)+
  labs(x = "age", y = "fertility rate", color = "union status")+
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-tfr-on-demand
#| fig-cap: Estimated mean total fertility rate over time from the simulation, separated by union status in comparison to input total fertility rates. Input total fertility rates are shown by dotted horizontal lines.

input_tfr <- bind_rows(
  fertility_rates_overall |> calculate_tfr() |> mutate(union_status = "overall"),
  fertility_rates_by_status |> calculate_tfr()
)


tfr |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = time_mid, y = tfr, group = union_status, color = union_status, fill = union_status))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_hline(data = input_tfr, aes(yintercept = tfr, color = union_status),
             linetype = 2)+
  labs(x = "time", y = "total fertility rate", color = "union status")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-tfr-on-demand summarizes the age-specific fertility rates by showing the total fertility rate by union status and overall across five year time periods. The results are consistent with the previous figures showing that the mean overall TFR is identical to the input TFR across all time periods, while the mean unpartnered TFR is forced to zero and the mean partnered TFR is slightly higher than the input data. 

Notably, the TFRs in all three cases are stationary across time except for the partnered case in the beginning of the simulation where it starts very high. This is because the entire population begins as unpartnered and only transitions to a partnered status with a birth, so the initial ratio of births to person-years lived as partnered is very high. This quickly reverts to an equilibrium level that is much closer to the partnered TFR from the input data although still higher. In general, the results here demonstrate that the on demand model should not be used to analyze fertility rates disaggregated by partnership status, as expected.

### Age specific marriage rates

Because the goal of the on demand model is to preserve overall fertility rates and not marriage rates,  I don't expect it to produce accurate marriage rates. Because unions occur when an unpartnered women gives birth and we do not yet allow union dissolution, the marriage rates observed in the simulation will closely match the rate of first births for women (with some moditification due to remarriages upon widowhood) and not actual marriage rates. However, it is useful to see how closely it tracks the actual marriage rates observed in the input data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mar-rates-on-demand
#| fig-cap: Estimated mean age specific marriage rates for women across 100 simulations and 20 time periods compared to age specific marriage rates for women from input data. Input rates are shown by dotted red line. 

mar_rates |>
  filter(sex == "f") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start + 2.5, y = rate))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  geom_line(data = mar_rates_female, linetype = 2, color = "red")+
  labs(x = "age", y = "marriage rate")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-mar-rates-on-demand shows the mean age-specific marriage rates for women from the simulations in comparison to those same races for the input data. As expected the two schedules differ somewhat. The observed marriage rates peak earlier and then decline faster than the input marriage rates. 

Because this result is dependent upon the fertility schedule, the degree of fit between these two sources will vary considerably across simulations depending on a variety of factors. Therefore, the results from @fig-mar-rates-on-demand should not be taken as a generalizable statement of the degree of agreement or disagreement expected when using the on demand model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gender-mar-rates-on-demand
#| fig-cap: Estimated mean age specific marriage rates for men and women across 100 simulations and 20 time periods.

mar_rates |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_start, y = rate, group = sex, color = sex))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x = "age", y = "marriage rate", color = "sex")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-gender-mar-rates-on-demand compares the mean age specific rates for women and men in the simulation. The two results are quite close, but the peak for men is lower and the decline is slower. This is expected because the model assumes a slight preference for women to marry older men.

### Share ever married

```{r}
#| label: create-ever-married-function

calc_ever_married <- function(result, age) {
  result$unions |>
    select(start_time, husband_id, wife_id) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = c(husband_id, wife_id), values_to = "person_id") |>
    group_by(person_id) |>
    summarize(mar_time = min(start_time), .groups = "drop") |>
    right_join(result$persons, by = "person_id") |>
    mutate(
      age_observed = pmin(death_time, result$end_time, na.rm = TRUE) - birth_time,
      age_mar = mar_time - birth_time
    ) |>
    filter(age_observed >= age) |>
    mutate(ever_married = !is.na(age_mar) & age_mar <= age) |>
    mutate(birth_decade = floor(birth_time / 10) * 10) |>
    group_by(sex, birth_decade) |>
    summarize(prop_ever_married = mean(ever_married), .groups = "drop")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ever-married-50
#| fig-cap: Mean proportion ever married by age 50 by ten-year birth cohorts that have reached 50 by the end of the simulation, across 100 simulations.

results_ondemand |> map(calc_ever_married, 50) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  group_by(sex, birth_decade) |>
  summarize(prop_ever_married = mean(prop_ever_married), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = birth_decade, y = prop_ever_married, group = sex, color = sex))+
  labs(x= "birth year", y = "proportion ever married by age 50")+
  geom_line()+theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ever-married-30
#| fig-cap: Mean proportion ever married by age 30 by ten-year birth cohorts that have reached 30 by the end of the simulation, across 100 simulations.

results_ondemand |> map(calc_ever_married, 30) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  group_by(sex, birth_decade) |>
  summarize(prop_ever_married = mean(prop_ever_married), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = birth_decade, y = prop_ever_married, group = sex, color = sex))+
  labs(x= "birth year", y = "proportion ever married by age 30")+
  geom_line()+theme_bw()
```

@fig-ever-married-50 and @fig-ever-married-30 show the proportion of men and women married across the 100 simulations by birth cohorts, excluding individuals who died before reaching the focal age and cohorts that had not reached that age by the end of the simulation. As expected this proportion is ero for cohorts who were old by the start of the simulation but rises quickly for cohorts in the marriageable ages. Once we reach cohorts born within the simulation, those proportions remain stationary for the remainder of the simulation. 

I have no prior expecation of what these proportions should be for this model aside from being reasonable values, which I judge them to be.
